newsitem.title: UK: GOLF-WOOSNAM RECOVERS FROM SHAKY START TO WIN.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-WOOSNAM RECOVERS FROM SHAKY START TO WIN.

text.p: Ian Woosnam of Britain overcame a faltering start before settling down on the back nine to win the British PGA title with a two-under-par final round of 70 on Monday.

The Welsh Ryder Cup veteran won by two strokes for his second victory in the championship after tasting success in 1988. He also took the World Matchplay title twice on the same course in 1987 and 1990.
"I didn't play my best golf today but I managed to get round. But the old heart was pumping a bit towards the end," he said.
"It wasn't one of my most spectacular rounds but it was one of my better chipping rounds. That kept me going."

South African Ernie Els and Nick Faldo of Britain both birdied the final hole for rounds of 70 to create a three-way tie for second with Irishman Darren Clarke, who could only par the long closing hole for a 71.
Woosnam, the 1991 U.S. Masters champion, finished on 275, 13 under par, to take the winner's cheque for 183,340 pounds ($300,000) and go top of the European Order of Merit.
Els, Faldo and Clarke finished on 277.
European number one Colin Montgomerie vaulted up to fifth place on 278 with an eight-under-par 64, the best of the week a day after he stumbled to a 76 in the third round.
Angel Cabrera of Argentina, with a 69, and Englishman David Gilford, after a 70, shared sixth place another shot behind on 279, nine under par.
Woosnam, who threw away the Desert Classic title in Dubai early in March when he pitched into a lake at the last hole, said memories of that shot came back to haunt him at the last hole on Monday.
He said he had a disagreement there with his long time caddie, Phil Morbey.
"He said hit a three wood, then a one iron. I was confused. I still felt Darren (Clarke) could eagle the hole so I didn't want to make five," he said.
"I finally hit a driver but I never committed to the shot and hooked it."
He finished in the rough, but played safely out, recovering to make par for victory when Clarke could do no better.
But Woosnam had virtually clinched his triumph with a birdie four at the previous hole, the 571-yard 17th. A perfect drive, a long iron just short and a perfect chip to one foot set it up.
Yet for a long time nothing went right. He missed four of the first five greens yet parred them all and made par on the first 11 holes before a 12-foot putt at the 12th brought his first birdie.
Then he rolled in a 25-footer at the short 14th for another birdie and Clarke, who had bogeyed the 13th, fell from one ahead after 11 to two behind.
Woosnam was never headed after that though Clarke matched his birdie at 17.
"It is good to beat a field as strong as this one. There was pressure at the end and I felt it, but I managed to come through it," he said.
"I threw Dubai away," Woosnam added. "But I've been second a couple of times since then and I played well at the Benson and Hedges International two weeks ago."
Clarke, the burly 28-year-old from Northern Ireland, had three birdies against a single bogey on the front nine as he took over the lead.
But at the 13th he missed the green and made a bogey five and two holes later he three-putted for another bogey.
Clarke, who won the German Masters late last year, is now third in the Ryder Cup table and sure of a European team place at Valderrama in September.
Faldo bemoaned missed chances on the back nine. "I could have birdied 10, 11, 12 and 13, I bogeyed 14, had half a chance at 17 and finally made one at 18, a 14-footer," he said.
Still, his trans-Atlantic quest for Ryder Cup points was not in vain for he moved up from 62nd to 20th place in the Cup standings with his second place finish.
